utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, Ms. Suzanna Mohr, and Ms. Alexandra Laskowski appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a matter to raise, but I'll wait until Your Honour has finish the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was just going to say before the witness was returned to the stand, we were alert that you may have had a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, good morning to you. Again for the record I remind you that you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, your expert's report in items 239 to 256, you speak about the co-operation between the military and the police. Page 18718 of the transcript contains your analysis of a document P1787, which is tab 34 in the Prosecution binder. It's footnote 321, 348, 455, and 720. I remind you that the discussion related to this document pertained mostly to the issue of co-ordinated action. Do you remember that? Do you remember that you spoke with Ms. Korner about that topic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, before we analyse this document, we are going to return to this document later, that's what I mean to say. But before that I think we owe it to the Trial Chamber and all the participants here in the courtroom to explain what exactly "co-ordinated action" means. Mr. Brown, co-ordinated action is a military term that denotes a method of the execution of a joint task wherein two or more units act in co-ordination towards achievement of a task assigned by their superior commander. Would you agree with this definition?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not solely a military term, I would argue, but it can be used in a military context clearly. And I would agree that it usually means two or more units acting together in order to achieve a common goal. It doesn't necessarily mean to say that it couldn't be two units, two organisations from different components, but I agree that there is a co-ordination component. There usually is multiple actors and they are acting normally in concert to achieve a common aim or a common goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The essence is that the co-ordinated action is ordered by a superior commander, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the actors involved can have their own command chain, and as I maybe mentioned when we were discussing this previously, you can have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, excuse me. I have to interrupt you. You did explain that and that is not in dispute. It is clear that the units have their own chains of command, but the essence here, what I'm now asking you about is the following: Somebody ordering a co-ordinated action of two units with two different chain of commands, that person, that individual or a command is superior to both those units then because that is the command that is in a position to order the co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the military unit taking part here, so this is a Kotor Varos light brigade unit, I would agree, yes, that I would imagine the corps command has instructed its subordinate formations to conduct operations. What others who are taking part in the operation may or may have not been asked to do, I do not know, but in relation to this military unit, I would suspect that its superior command has been made aware or it has instructed this unit to conduct operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us take an example. Let's take a look at P1787, tab 34. That's the document that you spoke about with Ms. Korner. Sir, this is a document dated 23rd of July, issued by the command of the Light Infantry Brigade Kotor Varos. I say that through this document the command of the light infantry brigade as a superior command orders its subordinated units defined in items 1 to 5 and item 8, orders them to execute a certain task. This document is signed by the commander of the Light Infantry Brigade Kotor Varos who is Mr. Manojlo Tepic. So the command of the Light Partisan Brigade is the superior command to all the units enumerated in items 5.1 to 5.8, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the companies that are under -- that form the core of the light brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, if we analyse this document, in particular its page 3 and onwards, we are going to see that out of 8 points in which the superior command of the Light Infantry Partisan Brigade Kotor Varos, that out of these 8 points, only in 5.2 and 5.3 we find units of the MUP. So out of 8, you have MUP in two points and not in six points; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's also a reference in paragraph 11 in relation to security support so presumably his security staff, but also a reference, acting in concert with neighbours and the police forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that, but now we are talking about the tasks assigned to the subordinated units, and that's item 5 in this order, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem from the documents that the 2nd Infantry Company, the pioneer platoon, and the security support staff of the brigade have been given tasks to co-ordinate or have some form of co-ordination with the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you answered a question posed by His Honour Judge Harhoff, page 18727 [Realtime transcript read in error "18727"] of the transcript, you said that this was a true subordination, resubordination of the police units to the army and if that were the case, then you said that you would have expected that they would have received specific and very explicit tasks in this order. Do you remember that you said something to this effect?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have expected if there was a police formation that was subordinated directly to this brigade, that I would see that replicated in one of the sub-formations and the tasks given to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am so sorry, can I have the page again of the transcript? It's come out as 1827.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 18721. Judge Harhoff asked how about the legal structure and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, so the tasks of the subordinated units, any task that would entail a co-ordinated action with the MUP units, we can find here only assigned to the two units, the pioneer platoon and the 2nd Infantry Company, is that true?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the security support staff. I'm presuming this brigade had some security personnel, security officers, security staff who conducted security tasks on behalf of the brigade, and they've also have a highlighted role. So those three components would seem to be the ones that are -- have been given this role of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that, I accept that. It is obvious that the police would have been involved with some sort of security aspect of this situation. However, I claim that items 5.2 and 5.3 give to the police a very explicit and very specific task or tasks such as with part of your forces acting in concert with the forces of the SJB Kotor Varos organised checking of unknown individuals and foreigners entering the area. So now, I don't know when you say this is not specific, in what way is it not specific? Do you think that this order should also contain a particular point where the check-point is to be set up in order to control the entry of unknown persons and foreigners? Do you think that they should tell them the exact geographical point where the check point should be and that only that would be sufficiently explicit and specific?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe point 5.2, the tasks given there, are specific tasks given to the police. I think this is a section that gives the tasks to the 2nd Infantry Company, the 2nd Infantry Company is to organise the checking of unknown individuals and foreigners entering the area in concert with the police. He is not instructing in this paragraph. It doesn't read the police contingent are to do the following. This paragraph refers to the tasks given to the 2nd Infantry Company, and I would imagine what has happened here is that there's been some co-ordination meeting where it's been agreed that both the 2nd Infantry Company will conduct the organised and checking of individuals and that the police will do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, with all due respect, I am kindly asking you to respond to my questions. The fact that you have your own understanding of what might have happened, which falls into the realm of speculation, this is contrary to what is written here. What is written here it says in a co-ordinated action with Kotor Varos SJB forces sets up control of the entry of unknown persons and foreigners. A moment ago we agreed the meaning of the phrase "co-ordinated action." Now I put it to you that both in this case and some other cases that we are going to review, the command of the Light Infantry Brigade ordering this co-ordinated action is a superior command both to the 2nd Infantry Company of its own and to the Kotor Varos SJB because this SJB, according to the law, was resubordinated to the army for the purpose of executing this task?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'd have to disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the next document to demonstrate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter document 2624, tab 19 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a directive of 6th of June 1992, issued by Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, and it's been issued by the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I've just been told that in the meantime this was entered into evidence and this is now P1794.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You refer to this document in your statement given in July of 2009, therefore I suppose that you have seen this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I hadn't seen this document when I wrote my report, but I think it was one of the documents referenced when I made my statement or reviewed some documents last year, I believe, or probably the year before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to take a look at this document which is entitled directive for further actions, and then in the first three or four paragraphs it specifies and portrays the prevailing situation, and in the remainder of the document we can read about the goals of this operation listed under A, B, C, and D. And then under item 5, they speak about tasks of the units, so let's look at that. That's on page 2 in Serbian. The last paragraph, item 5. And I suppose it's the next page in English as well. Sir, what you can see here is that this is about the tasks of the 1st Krajina Corps, and General Ratko Mladic says the 1st Krajina Corps, et cetera, in a co-ordinated action with the 2nd Krajina Corps and in a co-ordinated action with East Bosnia Corps. Unfortunately in the English translation, it says in concert with the 2nd Krajina Corps and co-action, which means that this is the document that gave rise to the problem that we pointed out because the word "Sadjestvo" was first translated as in concert and then second time it was translated as co-action. I think we have all agreed, including the CLSS, that the word "Sadjestvo" should always be translated as a co-ordinated action. Can you see this, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the task set the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is not in dispute that Ratko Mladic represents a higher command with regard to all the three corps, the 1st, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Main Staff which Ratko Mladic headed sat above those corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that's the point. Only a superior command is entitled to order a co-ordinated action to be carried out by units. In this particular instance, Ratko Mladic is not issuing an order to the 1st Krajina Corps as could have been inferred from your interpretation of the previous document, but rather issuing an order to the 1st, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and the East Bosnia Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the order is what it is. It's a directive from the command, the commander of the Main Staff, to subordinated corps, and those corps are to co-operate in a large operation in the corridor, well, there was Sarajevo as well, but that's what he is ordering. But the document is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, the essence is as follows: In this document regardless of the fact that initially the task is assigned to the 1st Krajina Corps, the Main Staff of the VRS is giving an order to the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps instructing them to act in a co-ordinated action together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So if in this case the co-ordinated action applies to all the listed units, why did you say with regard to the previous document that this did not apply to police units?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little bit unclear in your question. There's -- General Mladic is well within his right to ask, to order actually, his subordinate corps to co-ordinate together to conduct an operation in the corridor. The Kotor Varos Light Brigade orders its subordinate units in that operation, the various companies and support functions and platoons, to conduct operations, and one of the tasks it sets, one of its subordinate formations, is to co-ordinate with the police in Kotor Varos. I don't see that somehow the second one automatically implies that the Kotor Varos Light Brigade therefore commands all the police. I think there are two different tasks going on, but in this one, in this directive, Mladic is saying, and generally at the higher level the instructions are more general and they are larger, a number of corps are to co-operate together in order to conduct a large military operation. Now, what would likely follow from that is that each corps would look at the tasks set, look at the areas that it has to work with, have planning meetings with the corps that they have been told to co-operate with to come with up with a plan of action that would result in the execution of this order. Which I believe is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please concentrate on my question. First of all in this directive, Ratko Mladic, if you read it, as a superior command is issuing an order to subordinate units to carry out a co-ordinated action specifying exactly the tasks, and I'm not going into details of those tasks. Now, I put it to you, sir, that an entirely identical principle was applied in the tasks that we looked a moment ago assigned by the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, and the essence is that I'm telling you that when the command of Light Infantry Brigade says a co-ordinated action, that implies that at that point in time the police units are resubordinated to the army. Due to that, the commander of the Light Infantry Brigade can issue orders for co-ordinated actions to all units and hence all these units are under his command, just as was the case in the order issued by Ratko Mladic to the corps. If you still disagree with me, I can show you another document that would clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with you that the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade from this instruction has subordinated police units that it commands and it is giving instructions to. I do not see that from that document, and I do not believe that the Mladic document is anything other than a high level directive to subordinate corps to co-operate in the execution of a large military task in the corridor and also in relation to operations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us then look at a third document. I have a whole host of documents that can show that you are -- that you are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document 1D049216, that's the tab 34, footnote 134.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object again, and particularly in the light of the matter I raised this morning, to comments and remarks such as "I can show you a whole host of documents that will show you are wrong." That is pure comment. He can put what documents he likes and then thereafter make submissions at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Brown and to you, Ms. Korner. You are right. It was inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, this document that you deal with in your footnote 144 in your report is an order issued by the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 31st of July, 1992, and this order was given by the 1st Krajina Corps to its subordinate units as their superior command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Have you got a tab for that, sir, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 34 in the Defence binder, although I don't know if you have that particular binder with you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, sir. I probably know this is a rather large document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is. I don't know if you prefer -- I promise that over the break I'm going to prepare this document for you in English, and I don't think it will be helpful if I gave you my copy in the Serbian, but you are right and I'm going to instruct some people for all the documents that I intend to use in my cross-examination to be printed and hard copies given to you. Now, this document refers to the same issue, therefore I don't think you will have any difficulties in understanding both what is written in the document and my questions. Now, let's go to page 6 where it reads "I have decided ..." Actually, it's page 7, item 5.2, which starts with "I have decided ..." Item 5.2. Tasks of subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 7 in Serbian, and it is ERN number 0084-1213. Since there are some pages inserted, it could be then page 14. Thank you. That's the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, General Talic under item 5.2 refers to TG 2 and orders Tactical Group 2 as follows: "In coordination with Tactical Group 1 and Tactical Group 3 organises persistent and active defence applying massive barrier system," et cetera et cetera. You can see this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This means that here this section is entitled tasks of subordinated units, so there is no doubt that Tactical Groups 1, 2, and 3 are the units subordinated to General Talic's command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would seem so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. Item 5.3 on the next page, it talks about the tasks of Tactical Group 3, and it reads: "In co-ordination with Tactical Group 2 and the Srbac Light Brigade organise the defence," et cetera. In this instance again, Tactical Group 3 that is receiving the order and the units TG 2 and the Srbac Light Brigade are again units subordinated ... As I said, these units are yet again units subordinated to the General Talic's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. 5.6 on the next page. Now we have a Combat Group 2 and it reads: "In co-ordination with the 1st Detachment" -- and this task is being given to Combat Group 2, "In co-ordination with the 1st Detachment of Posavina Brigade, part of the IBK forces, and MUP forces, block the bridgehead established in the region of Orasje ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I can give you a hard copy of this document in English if the Usher would be so kind to help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we are talking about item 5.6.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that on the screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what one can see here is again a task given to MUP forces to take part in a co-ordinated action, and they are being given a very explicit and clear tasks such as block the bridgehead in the region of Orasje, then capture Orasje and a number of villages, and eventually reach the Sava river and organise defence there. You will agree with me that there is no doubt that the MUP forces are subordinated to the army in this particular instance, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you, sir. This section is an instruction to Combat Group 2. Talic is ordering Combat Group 2 which is a subordinate unit of his corps. He is not ordering the 1st Posavina brigade which I don't believe was part of his corps. He is not ordering the East Bosnia Corps, nor is he ordering the MUP. I believe what he is saying, he is ordering Combat Group 2 which is a subordinate formation to co-ordinate with these units which are not under his command in order to conduct this operation, I believe this is in the corridor area, and I would agree with you it would appear that the Posavina Brigade, the IBK forces, and the MUP forces are involved in combat operations there. But what he is doing is he is telling Combat Group 2 who clearly are going to be part of that operation, to co-ordinate with those other units in order to execute this particular task in this particular area. I don't know exactly where that is or whether it took place or what planning meetings may have gone on as a result of that, but in reading the document very briefly, I would have to say, General Talic is ordering his subordinate formation Combat Group 2 to co-ordinate with units that are not part of his corps, which would seem to be a recognised military task which goes on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, Mr. Brown, if what you are saying is true, how do you think, then, that this can function in reality? What I mean is I as General Talic, or I don't know who, issue an order to my subordinate unit to carry out a co-ordinated action with units that are not under his command and he expects them to execute this tasks. Is this what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say from my military experience, this happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neighbouring formations are conducting operations, different formations and different command with the same objective. It's happening now and it's happened in my military service, and I don't see this as an issue that surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But tell me this, sir: In your view how is it possible then for the Combat Group 2 to execute a co-ordinated action with East Bosnia Corps if they are not under the command of General Talic? One may expect the East Bosnian Corps to say no we are not going to comply and also the MUP forces could have said that, they could have just said no, these are not our tasks and our goals.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat Group 2 is under General Talic's command. Clearly Combat Group 2, I don't know the details of the group and I don't know what its task specifically, although you can read it from here, is, but clearly Combat Group 2 has been given a task by General Talic as part of this operation. I would assume, I don't know the East Bosnia Corps and I haven't seen the documents from the East Bosnia Corps, that it was probably quite likely that this, a similar instruction was given to the East Bosnia Corps in the same way the Directive 1 -- General Talic wrote his own directive as part of that operation. I would assume that a larger directive came from the Main Staff which also went to the East Bosnia Corps and that the East Bosnia Corps was to be part of a task in relation to this wider, I believe, corridor area. But what would then happen, normally what happens, is there's some kind of planning process in which it is agreed which units are going to take part and what their roles and responsibilities will be. So of course the East Bosnia Corps or the MUP could say we are not taking part in this, that's a different issue completely. They might decide that the task that they'd been set is too great for the forces they have, but that's why you have these planning formations. But I go back to my point, Combat Group 2 has been given instructions by General Talic to co-ordinate with units which do not fall under the 1st Krajina Corps hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, with all due respect, honestly I can say that at one point you have confirmed what I am alleging. There should be a superior command which sets out a task such as blocking a bridgehead in Orasje, capture Orasje, and reach the river Sava and organise defence. This must be set by a superior command. It is saying this to Talic, it is saying the same thing to East Bosnia Corps and also to the 2nd Krajina Corps, and then they pass on these orders to their subordinated units, including the resubordinated units of the MUP, because there must be a higher level command to issue this kind of order. You yourself said that there was a directive issued to that effect. Therefore, what I'm trying this whole time is to establish that a co-ordinated action involving a number of units is something that can be ordered only by a superior command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task given to Combat Group 2 clearly has been given by a superior command. It may well be that Combat Group 2 is the most important unit taking part in this operation, but when General Talic has been given his instruction by the Main Staff and he has done his staff planning, he decides that Combat Group 2 has to fulfill this task. And it may well be that he realises that there are other factors that in order for Combat Group 2 to succeed, that he requires additional support. He may, for example, feel that the flanks of Combat Group 2 are weak and that what he wants the East Bosnia Corps to do is to secure those flanks while Combat Group 2 take part in the operation. It may well be that when General Talic has done his appreciation, he realizes Combat Group 2 has to conduct this operation, but there are problems that require some assistance from the MUP or from the Posavina Brigade. And so what he's -- but it could also be that the main player in this is the East Bosnian Corps, but what he has done, he has -- he has given instructions to Combat Group 2 and he has clearly appreciated that there is a co-ordination requirement component involving these other actors that needs to be resolved and that's what he's instructing Combat Group 2 to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm asking about the principle of command and control in the army, and you are talking to me about specific operations. I'm taking these examples in order to show what it was like in the real world and in 1992 at that. But basically I'm talking about the principle involved. Please focus, please respond to those questions. I'm talking about the principle. In order for two units that have different commands to take part in co-ordinated action, a superior command has to give them an order for this co-ordinated action to both units involved and to set their objective. You go there together, don't you? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that is always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at 5.11 of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are still dealing with paragraph 5 where the late General Talic is setting the tasks for subordinated units. And now 5.11 pertains to the Banja Luka Light Brigade's group. You do remember saying that Mr. Talic -- I think that was your position, that he asked the Main Staff to establish this command of this group of the Banja Luka Light Brigade's group that was under the 1st Krajina Corps; right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the light brigades, there's no dispute there, they are under the Krajina Corps; that is to say, General Talic commands them and now is giving them a task. And this is what he says: "In co-ordination with the MUP forces and the 1st Krajina Corps units in the garrison, establish complete control" and so on and so forth. Now, this is what I'm putting to you: That these are all the units that he is giving an order to, the light brigades, the MUP forces, and the units of the 1st Krajina Corps and the garrison, that all of these units are subordinated to him and he is issuing them an order for co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, sir. He is ordering the Banja Luka Light Brigade's group to co-ordinate with the MUP and other units in the garrison to establish control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not ordering the MUP. He is ordering the Banja Luka group of light brigades to co-ordinate with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me then who is it that issues orders to the MUP forces to carry out this task, this very same task? Who is ordering the MUP forces to carry out this very same task with the light brigade's group and the units of the 1st Krajina Corps and the garrison, who is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert on the MUP and the chain of command of the MUP so I'm not sure, but I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I mean, Mr. Brown, I put a question to you and if you are say together me that you are not an expert and that you cannot respond to that question, there's no need for us to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that there probably had to be some co-ordination meeting with the senior MUP in Banja Luka, but I don't know the structures or how that would function.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, but even if there were this kind of co-ordination, which did not exist, somebody has to issue the order for that MUP organisation to carry out this task, that Talic is ordering his own units to carry out, isn't that right? It has to be a higher command, a superior command, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a higher police command, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this higher police command, who is it issuing orders to them, the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine there is a recognised chain of command in the MUP in the same way there was in a military, but I'm not an expert in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But now I'm asking you a question based on fundamental logic. If somebody issued an order to Mr. Talic to carry out this task, and then in order to carry out the order that he was given he is issuing an order to his own subordinate units; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is issuing an instruction here to [Overlapping speakers] ... Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You agree with that, so if that is on the left-hand side, if I can put it that way, the army is on the left-hand side and on the right-hand side it's the police, the MUP, and there had to be some kind of a higher MUP command telling the lower MUP command that this task should be carried out. That's your position right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. What might have happened here is that General Talic, in order to, whatever he is doing for the Banja Luka -- secure Banja Luka for all intents and purposes, in his assessment when he looks at that, he realises that the Banja Luka group of light brigades needs to do certain things and he realises he hasn't got the manpower or there are legal issues or it makes sense to have the police engaged in that, there might have been a planning meeting at the Banja Luka level to say can you assist in this, or we require your support in this, or we are going to be conducting an operation here in this particular area at this particular time, you need to be aware of this, is there anything that you need to do in that regard, or can we have your support in that. And it may well be that that planning meeting is enough, or it may well be that the MUP decide that no we have to have instructions from the senior level, or it may well be that this is a joint operation well known to the police and there is a similar type of instruction going on. I don't know. But what I do know is that General Talic clearly has identified a function and a role for the Banja Luka light brigades which in his assessment necessitates co-ordination with the police. How that co-ordination occurred, what requests may have been made, and the chain of command from the MUP is out with my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree, Mr. Brown, however, by the very logic of things somebody has to have authority over somebody else just as Talic has authority over his subordinate units in order to instruct them to carry out a particular task. The way you are interpreting things to us seems to show that Mr. Talic is establishing that he does not have enough soldiers, that he needs MUP support, and that then he goes somewhere and says please, give me a number of policemen so that we can carry out this task. And then somebody from the MUP says, no, I don't want to do that, and then that task is not carried out, although the task was issued by the supreme commander President Karadzic and it was then repeated by the Chief of the General Staff Ratko Mladic. So what do you think, if that were the situation, what would happen to General Talic? General Talic would not carry out the task that he was assigned and what happens then? He says to Ratko Mladic, sorry, Ratko, I could not carry out this task because these guys from the MUP said we don't want to. Do you seriously believe that that is the way things work in war time and would there be any logic for things to function that way?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of your question. All I can say is that from paragraph 5.11, General Talic is instructing his subordinate formations to establish complete control in the wider area of Banja Luka and in assessing that task and giving that task the brigade, he has set a role to co-ordinate with MUP forces. And it may well be that that -- I would imagine the MUP are establishing check-points and doing functions in Banja Luka and he realises that that needs to be co-ordinated with the police. That's my reading of this section. How that co-ordination happened, what chains of command the police have is really not something I can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now we are going to try to explain that as well. I would like to move for this document to be admitted, 1D24126?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D405, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we finished with this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, the problem is, Mr. Brown, that part of your paper that the Prosecution is trying to get admitted has to do with co-operation, it is entitled co-operation between the army and the police. And what is suggested there is that there was a certain way in which this co-operation was carried out. Although you are telling me that that was not part of your expertise, due to the reasons that I've just mentioned, namely this is included in your expert opinion that the Prosecution wishes to have admitted into evidence here, I have to set some things straight here with you irrespective of your expertise. After all, I think it was your duty to have a look at this documentation before you wrote this up or rather while you were writing it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a speech and its an improper speech. The witness is here to answer questions, his expertise he has always said is in the military side and the documents that relate to that. The purpose of cross-examination is to ask questions, not to make speeches like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Indeed, I note, Mr. Zecevic has continued to lapse into speeches, but we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I just wanted to give an explanation before the next set of document is given to -- is shown to the witness. In all fairness to the witness, that was the only purpose I tried to explain why I'm going to show him these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you moving on to something else and thus leaving the issue of co-operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D46. That is tab 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order of the Ministry of the Interior. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to be fair to the witness, I don't know if -- I assume that the witness has not seen a couple of the documents which I need to present to him. And I suggest the following: That we adjourn at this point, that I make the photocopy of the English versions of these documents, provide the witness that he can consult them during the break, and then when we return we can continue. That is my suggestion if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that seems eminently sensible. I suppose we should take our half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we discussed over the break the length of time that Mr. Brown is likely to be, and it seems to all of us that he is still going to be here on Friday morning at the rate we are going. I just wonder if somebody perhaps could mention it to him of Your Honours, so that if he has made any plans to get away, he may have to forget about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one intervention in the transcript at page 25 line 2, I offered the document, it's a 1D405 but the identification number I think was recorded wrong. It's a document 1D049216. And that is the document 1D405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zecevic continues, two matters. Notwithstanding the late start for this session, for the usual reasons we would have to take a break before we rise for the day and after discussions with the Court Officer, we'll take that break at 12.30. The second thing, Mr. Brown, counsel, plural, have asked me to alert you that their sense of the progress of your cross-examination, continued cross-examination, re-examination, means that your testimony is -- will certainly extend into Friday. So that such arrangements as you would have made, you could bear that in mind. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, is it likely to finish on Friday or is it likely to extend after that? I only say because I have some commitments which I would like to sort of honour this weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My impression from what counsel -- of what counsel said is that it will finish on Friday, but could I have counsel confirmation on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will endeavour to finish today, but I might really have a little bit of time tomorrow, and it is my assessment that knowing what we discussed between us, I believe that it is very likely that the witness -- Mr. Brown will finish on Friday, that is only from the point of the counsels. Of course, if the Trial Chamber has the questions, that's a different matter, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I'm reminded that we have a firm fixture for videolink on Monday. So it appears, Mr. Brown, that every effort will be made to ensure that your testimony is completed by Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, in order to put everything into the right context could you be shown again 1D004042; that is, the Law on Total National Defence that we looked at yesterday. We commented on it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Article 104 that I would like to see. I'm not sure what page that is in e-court. I'll try. It's page 18 and 67. It's 18 in Serbian and 67 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, Article 104 says in paragraph 2: "During its engagement for combat activities in the armed forces, the police shall be under the command of the authorised officer in charge of the combat activity." And in paragraph 1, it says that: "The police may also be used for carrying out combat activities for the armed forces in accordance with the law." Remember that we looked at it yesterday and commented upon it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the Law of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the law that was in force at the time in the territory of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert, but I don't believe that was. The RS began to implement and issue their own instructions and laws, so I'm not sure that 1982 Law on All People's Defence was still functioning in relation to Republika Srpska or Bosnia at that time but again I defer to a constitutional legal expert, but in my view I don't think this law was, certainly de facto, did not seem to be in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is the constitution of Republika Srpska and the Law on the Implementation of the Constitution. It's a constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution; however, let's not comment upon that now because this goes beyond your expertise. It is contained in the documents that make up our legal library.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 1D146, tab 154. 1D46, I apologise. That's the document that we had a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you something before we move on to this document. It is a fact, isn't it, that when we looked at those directives of the Main Staff that were signed by General Ratko Mladic, these directives were sent only to army units; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check the distribution but I think they did only go to the corps. I don't know if they also went to the Presidency or other people above him, but in terms of going down I think it was only to the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want us to waste time now so I'm not going to show you these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, for the purposes of the transcript, it is P1780 and P -- just a moment, please, P1794. In both documents, or rather it is obvious on the basis of both documents that this was only sent to the units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, another general question before I move on to the original question that I wanted to put. You know that in Republika Srpska the supreme commander was the president, Mr. Karadzic, and that according to the Law on the Army, he was the only one who had the right of command and that he could transfer that right to the Chief of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic, you do know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the Law of the Army. I would like to refresh myself if that's exactly the case, but in general I think that's probably true, whether it's the president of the Presidency or whether it's the president, I am not sure I would have to refresh myself, but clearly the president of the Presidency had that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Sir, in this document, paragraph 7, that's a document of the ministry dated the 15th of May, 1992. I don't know whether you've seen it before, however, on page 2 in paragraph 7, subparagraph 3, it says: "While participating in combat operations, the units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces," which is in accordance with the Law on Total National Defence which we saw a few moments ago; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. The language is slightly different. I think in the setting aside the issue of whether the Law on All People's Defence was relevant -- in 1982 was relevant at this time, I think Article 104 says they may be subordinate or they may be involved in combat operations. Here this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when they are carrying out combat operations they are subordinated to the officer in charge, that is what the law says; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what 104 says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this order simply copied the text of the law in this part; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether they copied it or whether they used it as a guide or whether it was something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that. Sir, during the direct examination you looked at P1789, that is Prosecution tab 24. Number 24. That is an order of the command to the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 19th of June, 1992. It is footnote 357 in your expert opinion, and you analysed this briefly with Ms. Korner, if I remember correctly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think Ms. Korner mentioned in reference this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is what this order says. Use of police in armed combat operations, and then it says: "Order: "In the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, there are different ways in which the police can be used in armed combat operations in order to overcome the problems involved. I hereby issue the following order." And then Mr. Talic says in paragraph 1 what the general tasks are that the police is carrying out in accordance with the Law on the Interior. Do you agree with what I've read out so far?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document seems to reflect that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 2 as opposed to the interpretation that was given during your direct examination, Mr. Talic says: "The police may be used in direct combat operations on the front only exceptionally when it is necessary to hold and strengthen the front line until the arrival of military units." And then paragraph 3: "In other cases," I emphasise that part, "In other cases it is necessary to inform the chief of the Security Services Centre and receive his approval." Sir, this document seems to indicate the following: First of all, in the preamble it says that there are different ways in which the police can be used and because of this variety of ways in which the police can be used, Mr. Talic is issuing this order. Do you agree with me up to this point?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he has written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 2 and 3 in essence Mr. Talic says: For direct combat operations, the police may be used without informing MUP organs and without receiving their approval if that is what the situation is at the front line. In all other cases, however, it is necessary to inform the MUP organs and to receive their approval; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he has written in the document, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So there's a clear distinction, isn't there, between a situation when the military due to its own opinion for the needs that exist in the front line may engage the police, and on the basis of this it seems that Mr. Talic is saying that in that case it is not necessary to ask for anyone's approval or to provide information to that effect to anyone; whereas, in all other cases for carrying out planned operations, that is, one has to provide information to that effect to the ministry and to ask for their approval. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would read this as bearing in mind the context of the time, and this comes in the middle of the corridor operation, but this is relating to front line, I think I maybe have mentioned this in direct, front line combat tasks, for example, that were occurring in the corps at that time in the corridor, and that in exceptional circumstances, presumably he means here if there is a weakness in the front line or if there's a counter-attack by the enemy formation, that in exceptional circumstances police can be used, but there are limitations and that they are to hold and strengthen the front prior to the arrival of military units. So in essence it's to plug a front line if there is a problem. And in other cases, informing chief of CSB -- an approval by the CSB is required, presumably reflecting some of the documents and the situation as seem to have been in late May when there are, I think, General Talic made a passing instruction that police had -- you know, that authority had to be sought from the CSB. So I read this document in the context of what was happening in the corridor and in the context that if the front is weak or there is a problem there, that police in exceptional circumstances can be used but they are to be used in essence in a limited way until the arrival of military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Brown, this document is dated the 19th of June, but it does not refer to the corridor at all, you can see that from the document itself. On the other hand, the front line does not exist only at the corridor, right? There is a front line on the western side of the Krajina, Skender Vakuf, Kljuic, Kotor Varos, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the main -- the main combat, if you like, front that Talic was concerned about at this time was especially the corridor, and I accept you are right there was a front line with central Bosnia which there was, if you like, combat activities against Croatian forces in central Bosnia so that was an area that he was concerned with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, less than 12 days after this document, on the 1st of June, 1992, the very same General Talic and the same command of the Krajina Corps issue a new order, 1D049057. In your report, the footnote is 358 and the Defence tab is number 14.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you check the tab again sir because I don't have that as number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Defence tab 14, Defence, not the Prosecution. I think that this document should be included in the documents you received during the break that had been photocopied for you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I think it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document is also one of the documents that you commented with Ms. Korner. On page 2, item 11, the third paragraph from the bottom in Serbian, I think that is the next page in English. It says: "As determined by in this order the exclusive right to command and employee units rest with the zone commander." And further on: "In the conduct of combat activities, all," and I emphasise, "all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander who shall decide how they are used." Sir, in your report, 2.50, page 82, you yourself say that this order of the 1st of July is obviously contrary to the instruction of the 19th of June, 1992, the document we've just looked at; is that right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document on its own with that instruction, I think I highlight it in the report, seems to be a change, it's not necessarily contrary, I guess, but it seems to indicate at least at that time and in this instruction a change from one that requires the approval of the CSB and a procedure by which police are to -- can be used in combat operations. Why this came about, I do not know. I do not know if there was some agreement that had been reached. I don't know what the discussions were prior to this. I can't say. But as I think I highlight in the reports, it's the only document actually I saw in the Krajina Corps that referenced this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said on page 18732. You said that that was the only document that you saw with such clear formulation. You said something to that effect. However, may I give you another suggestion in this enumeration of things that gave rise to this document. You will agree that there is also a possibility that this document is the first in a series of documents that we are going to look at which actually reflects the legal situation which army had not respected up to that point, or maybe they hadn't respected it in full?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a legal expert but I think I can say that prior to this this was not what was happening. Prior to this instruction, I did not see that zone commanders were -- had police units placed under their command, they were in essence deciding how they were going to be used. I didn't see that in any of the mobilisation instructions or establishment instructions being required by General Talic. I didn't see that in any of the combat reports that that was happening, and I didn't see that in things like directive that had common relation to the corridor. So certainly prior to the 1st of July, I did not see that happening. I have to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that post the 1st of July I didn't see it happening either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We are going to take a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D049057, tab 14, footnote number 358 in the expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you document 1D99. That is the order by the supreme commander that bears the same date, 1st of July. Could the usher please assist you, I think that this is one of the documents that we had added to our list subsequently and it may have not been photocopied for you. It's just a single page. I think that it won't be a problem for you to take a look at it now. That's 1D99. Here you can see that the president of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, on the 1st of July, 1992, says: "On the basis of my constitutional powers as the supreme public commander of the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on behalf of the Presidency of the SR Bosnia and Herzegovina, I hereby issue the following order," and what he is ordering is that two platoons of police forces should be resubordinated to a military unit. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Special Police. Sorry, Your Honour, I'm reading Special Police, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Special Police is also part of the police. It's a brigade within the Ministry of the Interior. I don't think that there is a need to burden the witness with those details right now. The details that he doesn't know enough about, but that's certainly not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what the document says, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to show you the following document, 1D100. That's an intervention or rather a memo sent by the minister about this order given by the supreme commander. Tab 145.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that one within the binder that was given me at the break, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That is correct, yes. [Interpretation] That's a document by the minister dated the 6th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have that one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that the copies have been given to you, but you can take a look at it on the screen in front of you. It's just a single page. In this document which refers to the previous document - that is the order by the supreme commander about the resubordination, specifically two platoons from the Special Police brigade of the Serbian MUP - the minister asks and reports that the order had been executed in accordance with the law and the constitution, that they had been resubordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, however, because of the need for them to carry out their tasks in accordance with the Law on the Interior, he requests that these policemen should be returned in order to perform their normal duties. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he clearly feels a need to come back to perform other duty and the tasks should be given to the army, I believe, is that my reading of the document? I think that seems to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Sir, the next document is 1D76 dated 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that's a memo sent from MUP and signed by Mr. Mico Stanisic. And here it says that during the first meeting of the MUP collegium held on the 11th of July, 1992, it was concluded that briefings should be prepared for a meeting with army representatives. And then further on under (b) it says that: "Data information regarding police involvement in those combat actions where their involvement was not necessary should be gathered." And then it says it should include the number of policemen involved in combat actions break down by month, April to July, and for the sake of comparison, the number of policemen who continue to work at their regular jobs within the domain of the MUP during the same time. Sir, this document shows us that on the 11th of July on the first collegium of the MUP of Republika Srpska meeting of their executives, a problem arose related to the involvement of the police with the military and their inability -- the inability of the police because of the lack of manpower to perform the normal duties defined by law. And that is why they request first, to solve the situation, to clear it with the army, and second, they want to have data that they could use in support of their request. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly the issue of the amount of time that the police are spending in combat operations would seem to be a concern there, and what they want to do is to find out facts on the ground about what is the case; how many policemen were involved and how many were not while doing presumably regular police jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm aware that you didn't see these documents in sufficient quantities and that is the reason that I cannot continue with my questioning about this.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've seen the document, so I've only just had a brief overview of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm going to show you something else in order to illustrate that the situation which was very problematic and caused concern to the MUP of Republika Srpska, that this situation continued. I'm going to show you P1094, that's footnote 360. That's a document that you looked at before. This is a document coming from the CSB in Banja Luka signed by Mr. Zupljanin. Tab 52. Okay. I think I also got it on the ... This document also speaks about the resubordination of the organs and members of the MUP to the army in its last paragraph, and they relate the wording of the law and the contents of the order of the 15th of May, which we looked at, saying that the police members may be engaged in combat activities according to the principle of resubordination to the superior army command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that they can't be used in territories outside their own areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is obvious that there isn't a unity of opinion between the police and the military about the number of the members of the MUP that had been resubordinated to the army during that period, which is for the most of 1992. So notwithstanding the law and the orders that we have examined, this problem was obviously an acute one. In order to illustrate that, I'm going to show you P427, item 8. It's tab number 7. That's a document that you received during the break. And that is information of the Ministry of the Interior dated 17th July, 1992. It was addressed to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister. At the very beginning, page 3 of this document, I think this is the previous page in English, you can see the following in the second paragraph in Serbian beginning with the words "first of all." Excuse me, I can't find it in English. The page that I need has number 0324-6857. That's the corresponding page to our Serbian page. Page 2, second paragraph from the bottom they tell me. Yes, I found it, yes. Here the ministry points out to the supreme commander and the prime minister that there is a problem, and they say this has mostly to do with the fact that the police are still on the first combat lines, for instance 100 per cent in Herzegovina, over 70 per cent in the Doboj region, et cetera, although this was justified at the beginning, and that there had been some talks of them being included into the military police during the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you read the whole paragraph there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm reading the whole paragraph in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it's completely -- it's coming out differently in English from what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am really sorry. [Interpretation] One of the participants in the debate described this graphically questioning the legitimacy of the police because "the army is in the streets controlling traffic, and police are in the trenches."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a problem here because there's quite a significant part in the English translation which we are all looking at which has not come out in the translation from what Mr. Zecevic read out. After the words: "This was justified in the beginning, or that the army keeps civilian police within its ranks after their agreed engagement" is how the translation is in English and has not been translated from what Mr. Zecevic read out, which is why I asked him to read the whole paragraph. Now, whether that's because the translators couldn't keep up with the speed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to read it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "This has mostly to do with the fact that the police are still on the first combat lines, 100 per cent in Herzegovina, over 70 per cent in the Doboj region, although this was justified at the beginning, or that the army keeps civilian police within its ranks after their agreed engagement in combat activities as part of military police units: All this affects the discharge of their regular duties and tasks." And I think that the rest was interpreted properly. Sir, this shows another problem or rather the identical problem that the police is trying to suggest to the supreme commander and the prime minister, and that is that because of the engagement of the police forces on front lines, they are unable to carry out their normal duties defined by the law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to be a problem that once the police had agreed to dispatch policemen to combat zones, that the army was keeping them there and that in some areas that this was a problem, so I agree, certainly, this looks like an issue that they are concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In essence, it means that there is no agreement because if there is an agreement -- or maybe that there is an agreement which is not being observed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem that there clearly has been the agreement that the process should be that there's a co-ordination, there's an agreement for how many need to go, and presumably for how long, and that in some cases, I mean, I can't talk about Herzegovina, I don't know that area at all, but Doboj I know was a big conflict zone, became more prevalent in the corridor operations, and that in that area the military are not, at least at face value, not honouring that agreement there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a concrete example. Now that you mentioned the area of Doboj, the Doboj municipality, it is also mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show 1D263 to the witness. It's tab 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document written by the chief of the centre and it is addressed to the operations group command of the Serbian Army. Single page. It's just one page. You see that it is dated 2nd of October, 1992, and in the document, the chief of the centre informs that due to the security situation in the area of the Serbian municipalities of Doboj, Derventa, and Modrica, they are forced to withdraw the police from the front line on the 4th of October, 1992. Then he gives the reasoning. He says that he hopes that the Serbian Army operations group command will correctly understand the reasons because of which he is forced to withdraw the police from the battle-field. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is perfectly in line with the document that we just looked at which said that 70 per cent of the police in the Doboj region is engaged on the battle-field. It seems that it was precisely the security situation within the territory that made the police to withdraw their members from the battle-field; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 70 per cent bit I'm not sure you can necessarily draw, because I think that instruction is some months before so this is a little bit later, but clearly they -- there are these other issues that they want to -- appear to want to deal with and so they want to withdraw their police. Presumably these are municipalities that were successfully taken in operation corridor, Derventa, Modrica, and the likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this, we commented somewhat on this yesterday, and we said that Colonel Slavko Lisica was the commander of the operations group of the Serbian Army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I forget if it was Tactical Group 1 or 3, but he was tactical group commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just as an example, I'm going to show to you document 1D264 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, I would like to ask a question. Mr. Brown, if this -- in this instance there would have been a formal resubordination decision as we saw a few documents ago coming from the highest echelons of the republic, could then the police - and here it's signed for the chief of the centre - unilaterally withdraw the resubordinated units from the army? Was it in his power to do so if there was a formal resubordination decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my experience much of that would depend on the agreement that was made prior to the operation being conducted. I don't doubt that the police could in certain circumstances be subordinated to military formations. I didn't see much of it. Most of it was in relation to co-operation and on-going operations where they would seem to play their part. But a lot of it would be dependent on what was agreed prior to the inclusion of these police in the military operations and that would undoubtedly involve agreement with superior commands in both. So I can't tell you whether for this particular operation the police that were involved in the tactical group that was in Doboj, which presumably was related to on-going operations in expanding the corridor and control of territory in that area, I can't tell you from this document whether the police were allowed to unilaterally withdraw. It may, for example, have been that the agreement to involve the police, setting aside what they were going to do specifically, but the agreement had a time-period that they were to be subordinated for a period, and at the end of that period they were to withdraw, and if the military kept them, the commander might have been well within his rights to remove them. So much depends on what the agreement was and that's what happens in planning meetings and co-ordination meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that resubordination decisions, as they can follow from the law, are made on the basis of agreements between the police and the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would expect they would be. It might be different if it was related to military formations, because clearly they're -- the Law on the Army, unity of command, but even in relation to, from my experience, where other army units are resubordinated, they usually are agreed periods of time, roles and responsibilities, some issues don't necessarily, you know, for example, disciplinary issues may not apply. But in relation to police, I would imagine there is a planning component and there's an agreement in relation to what these police will do and how long they will be there for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And agreed by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Agreed by the -- through the police chain and through the police command and agreed through the military chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are now going to look at document 1D264, which is in fact a response to the letter that we have just seen. It was sent by the commander, Colonel Lisica, and in which there's a detailed explanation of the relationship between the chief of the public security centre and the commander of the Doboj tactical group. We've seen that the previous document was dated the 2nd October, and this one is dated the 3rd October. And it is entitled "Withdrawing of Police Force from Combat Operations - Response" sent to Doboj CSB, and the commander, Colonel Lisica, says as follows: "I have understood your proposal and I underline your proposal regarding the withdrawal of police forces from combat operations." And then he goes on to say two or three sentences down: "I do not authorise the withdrawal of the police forces." So, sir, it is obvious who the superior commanding officer is in this situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he clearly doesn't believe that they should be withdrawn and he authorises it in his opinion they shouldn't be withdrawn. He doesn't order in this respect or make it clear that these police are to be ordered to stay, but clearly he believes that they shouldn't and he has a disagreement between the two and he authorises that they shouldn't be, so they are presumably within his unit and clearly there's a tension between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are both reading from the same document. How explicit should one be in an order issued by a superior officer if he says quite clearly and unequivocally I do not authorise the withdrawal of the police? He is writing to the CSB Doboj chief and says, I have considered your proposal and I do not allow and I do not authorise. Sir, it is quite clear that Colonel Lisica in this situation is a direct superior officer, and it's up to him whether the police would be pulled out of combat operations or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he clearly believes he has that authority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that both this document 1D263 and 264 have the designation MFI removed from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may not recall, but these two documents were the subject of some considerable discussion a very long time ago. The page numbers go from in the transcript 9949 through to 53 because it's evident, and this was the discussion that was raised, that these documents which have not been seen by the OTP before, come from some kind of a bound book. You may -- I think the discussion may come back to you when you look at the bottom of -- we need the -- yeah.
